definition.text: The basic physical laws governing energy, heat, work, temperature and entropy, which rule out things such as perpetual motion machines.

facts.text: Thermodynamics traditionally recognises three laws, with a more basic 'zeroth law' defining thermal equilibrium and temperature added later.
The first law says energy cannot be created or destroyed; the second says the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases.
The first two laws rule out machines that make work without energy input, and machines that turn heat spontaneously into work.
The first and second laws were established by 1860 through Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson.
Ecological economics uses the first and second laws to build economic models that respect physical limits; by these laws a perpetual motion economy is impossible.

definition.text: The law that natural processes are irreversible: the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases, so heat never flows by itself from cold to hot.

facts.text: Its simplest form, the Clausius statement, is that heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder to a hotter body.
All natural processes are irreversible; reversible processes are only a theoretical limit.
It was first formulated by Sadi Carnot in 1824 in his study of the motive power of fire.
Georgescu-Roegen called it the 'entropy law' and made it central to his economics.

title: Metabolic rift

definition.text: A theory, credited by sociologist John Bellamy Foster to Karl Marx, that capitalism breaks the natural exchange of materials between society and nature, producing ecological crisis.

facts.text: Foster, not Marx, coined the term, starting with his book Marx's Ecology.
Marx wrote during England's 'second' agricultural revolution (1815–1880), when soil exhaustion pushed Britain to import bone and guano for fertiliser.
It drew on Justus von Liebig's 1840 explanation of how soil nutrients feed plant growth.
Nutrients sent to cities as food were not returned to the land as waste, a one-way 'robbing of the soil' that linked urban pollution with soil depletion.
Originally a critique of capitalist agriculture, it has been extended to marine ecology and to a 'carbon rift' from rising carbon dioxide emissions.
Foster sees in it evidence that Marx held an ecological outlook, against claims that Marx ignored nature.

contested_note: Historical materialists such as Jason W. Moore read the rift's origins and nature very differently from Foster.
distinct_from: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift

title: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift

definition.text: Jason W. Moore's view that metabolic rifts began with capitalism in the 'long' 16th century and recur in each phase of capitalist development.

facts.text: Moore holds that the split between social and natural systems is empirically false and arbitrary.
He traces the rift to capitalist relations based on the law of value rather than to industrial agriculture.
James O'Connor sees capitalist undervaluing of nature leading to economic crisis, the 'second contradiction of capitalism'.

contested_note: Moore's view diverges widely from Foster's on what causes ecological crisis.

title: Eco-urbanism and the metabolic rift

definition.text: Efforts in city planning to close loops by bringing a city's energy, water, food and waste flows back within its own systems.

facts.text: The aim is greater self-reliance through 'closed-loop systems' that reduce dependence on outside networks.
Critics link it to 'managerial environmentalism' and doubt sustainable cities are feasible within global capitalism.

distinct_from: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift

definition.text: Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism: an accounting method for analysing social-ecological systems and simulating possible development paths.

facts.text: It keeps assessments consistent across scales and across economic, demographic and energy dimensions measured in different units.
It tracks who uses which resources and why, the resulting environmental pressures, and how far needs and pressures are shifted abroad through trade.
Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi created it around 1997 at the Autonomous University of Barcelona.
It suits analysis of the nexus between food, energy, water and land use, and has been tested with the FAO.
